questions.pyqTag: IIT JAM CY Topic • Physical Chemistry III: Chemical Kinetics, Electrochemistry & Adsorption (Set 01)
questions.questionTextEn: Which of the following statements correctly distinguishes the order and molecularity of a chemical reaction?
optionsEn: Molecularity is always equal to the sum of stoichiometric coefficients in the overall balanced equation.
Order of a reaction cannot change with experimental conditions such as pressure or reactant excess.
Order is always a positive integer, whereas molecularity can be zero or fractional.
Molecularity applies only to elementary steps and is always a positive integer, whereas overall order is experimentally determined and may be zero or fractional.
questions.explanationEn: Molecularity is the number of reactant species colliding simultaneously in a single elementary step, so it is always a positive integer (1, 2, or rarely 3). Overall reaction order is an empirical exponent in the rate law and can be zero, fractional, negative, or condition-dependent.

questions.pyqTag: IIT JAM CY Topic • Physical Chemistry III: Chemical Kinetics, Electrochemistry & Adsorption (Set 01)
questions.questionTextEn: Potassium chloride ($\text{KCl}$) is commonly chosen as the electrolyte in a salt bridge because
optionsEn: $\text{KCl}$ reacts with both electrodes to increase the cell EMF.
$\text{K}^+$ and $\text{Cl}^-$ have nearly equal ionic mobilities (transport numbers $\approx 0.5$), minimizing the liquid junction potential.
$\text{KCl}$ prevents any ion migration between the two half-cells.
$\text{K}^+$ has a much higher reduction potential than all transition metals.
questions.explanationEn: Because $\lambda^\circ(\text{K}^+) = 73.5$ and $\lambda^\circ(\text{Cl}^-) = 76.3\text{ S cm}^2\text{ mol}^{-1}$ are nearly equal ($t_+ \approx t_- \approx 0.5$), $\text{K}^+$ and $\text{Cl}^-$ diffuse out of the salt bridge at almost identical rates, maintaining electrical neutrality while minimizing the liquid junction potential.

questions.pyqTag: IIT JAM CY Topic • Physical Chemistry III: Chemical Kinetics, Electrochemistry & Adsorption (Set 01)
questions.questionTextEn: For the hydrogen electrode $\text{H}^+(\text{aq}) + e^- \rightleftharpoons \frac{1}{2}\text{H}_2(\text{g}, 1\text{ bar})$ at $298\text{ K}$, increasing the solution $\text{pH}$ by $2$ units changes its reduction potential by
questions.explanationEn: At $298\text{ K}$ and $p_{\text{H}_2} = 1\text{ bar}$, $E(\text{H}^+/\text{H}_2) = E^\circ - 0.0591\,\text{pH} = -0.0591\,\text{pH}$. Increasing $\text{pH}$ by $2$ units changes $E$ by $-2 \times 0.0591 = -0.118\text{ V}$.

questions.pyqTag: IIT JAM CY Topic • Physical Chemistry III: Chemical Kinetics, Electrochemistry & Adsorption (Set 01)
questions.questionTextEn: When $\log_{10} k$ is plotted against $1/T$ for a reaction obeying the Arrhenius equation $k = A\exp(-E_a/RT)$, the slope of the resulting straight line is
questions.explanationEn: Taking base-10 logarithms of $k = A e^{-E_a/RT}$ gives $\log_{10} k = \log_{10} A - \frac{E_a}{2.303\,R}\left(\frac{1}{T}\right)$. Hence the slope of $\log_{10} k$ versus $1/T$ is $-E_a / (2.303\,R)$.

questions.pyqTag: IIT JAM CY Topic • Physical Chemistry III: Chemical Kinetics, Electrochemistry & Adsorption (Set 01)
questions.questionTextEn: For a first-order reaction, the ratio of the time required for $75\%$ completion ($t_{3/4}$) to the half-life ($t_{1/2}$) is
questions.explanationEn: For a first-order reaction, $t = \frac{1}{k}\ln\left(\frac{[A]_0}{[A]_t}\right)$. At $75\%$ completion, $[A]_t = 0.25[A]_0 = [A]_0/4$, so $t_{3/4} = \frac{\ln 4}{k} = \frac{2\ln 2}{k} = 2 t_{1/2}$. Thus $t_{3/4}/t_{1/2} = 2.0$.

questions.pyqTag: IIT JAM CY Topic • Physical Chemistry III: Chemical Kinetics, Electrochemistry & Adsorption (Set 01)
questions.questionTextEn: The first-order gas-phase decomposition $A(\text{g}) \to 2B(\text{g}) + C(\text{g})$ is carried out in a rigid vessel at constant temperature. If the initial pressure of pure $A$ is $P_0$ and the total pressure at time $t$ is $P_t$, the first-order rate constant $k$ is given by
optionsEn: $\dfrac{1}{t}\ln\left(\dfrac{3P_0}{3P_0 - P_t}\right)$
$\dfrac{1}{t}\ln\left(\dfrac{P_0}{2P_0 - P_t}\right)$
$\dfrac{1}{t}\ln\left(\dfrac{2P_0}{2P_0 - P_t}\right)$
$\dfrac{1}{t}\ln\left(\dfrac{2P_0}{3P_0 - P_t}\right)$
questions.explanationEn: If partial pressure $x$ of $A$ decomposes, then $P_A = P_0 - x$, $P_B = 2x$, $P_C = x$, so $P_t = P_0 + 2x \implies x = (P_t - P_0)/2$. Hence $P_A = P_0 - \frac{P_t - P_0}{2} = \frac{3P_0 - P_t}{2}$, giving $k = \frac{1}{t}\ln\left(\frac{P_0}{P_A}\right) = \frac{1}{t}\ln\left(\frac{2P_0}{3P_0 - P_t}\right)$.

questions.pyqTag: IIT JAM CY Topic • Physical Chemistry III: Chemical Kinetics, Electrochemistry & Adsorption (Set 01)
questions.questionTextEn: A quinhydrone electrode ($E^\circ = +0.699\text{ V}$ vs. SHE at $298\text{ K}$) dipped in an acidic buffer shows a reduction potential of $+0.463\text{ V}$ vs. SHE. Taking $\frac{2.303RT}{F} = 0.0591\text{ V}$, the $\text{pH}$ of the buffer is closest to
questions.explanationEn: For the quinhydrone half-cell ($\text{Q} + 2\text{H}^+ + 2e^- \rightleftharpoons \text{H}_2\text{Q}$ with $[\text{Q}] = [\text{H}_2\text{Q}]$), $E = E^\circ - 0.0591\,\text{pH}$. Hence $\text{pH} = \frac{0.699 - 0.463}{0.0591} = \frac{0.236}{0.0591} = 3.99 \approx 4.0$.

questions.pyqTag: IIT JAM CY Topic • Physical Chemistry III: Chemical Kinetics, Electrochemistry & Adsorption (Set 01)
questions.questionTextEn: A Lineweaver–Burk plot of $1/v_0$ vs. $1/[S]$ for an enzyme at $[E]_0 = 2.0 \times 10^{-8}\text{ M}$ has a $y$-intercept of $2.5 \times 10^{4}\text{ M}^{-1}\text{ s}$ and a slope of $5.0\text{ s}$. The turnover number $k_{\text{cat}}$ and Michaelis constant $K_M$, respectively, are
questions.explanationEn: From $\frac{1}{v_0} = \frac{1}{V_{\max}} + \frac{K_M}{V_{\max}}\frac{1}{[S]}$: $V_{\max} = 1/(2.5 \times 10^4) = 4.0 \times 10^{-5}\text{ M s}^{-1}$. Thus $k_{\text{cat}} = V_{\max}/[E]_0 = (4.0 \times 10^{-5})/(2.0 \times 10^{-8}) = 2.0 \times 10^3\text{ s}^{-1}$, and $K_M = \text{slope} \times V_{\max} = 5.0 \times 4.0 \times 10^{-5} = 2.0 \times 10^{-4}\text{ M}$.

questions.pyqTag: IIT JAM CY Topic • Physical Chemistry III: Chemical Kinetics, Electrochemistry & Adsorption (Set 01)
questions.questionTextEn: According to the Debye–Hückel–Onsager equation $\Lambda_m = \Lambda_m^\circ - (A + B\Lambda_m^\circ)\sqrt{c}$ for strong electrolytes in dilute aqueous solution, the term $A\sqrt{c}$ and the term $B\Lambda_m^\circ\sqrt{c}$ account respectively for
optionsEn: the electrophoretic effect and the relaxation (asymmetry) effect
electrode polarization and concentration overpotential
the relaxation (asymmetry) effect and the electrophoretic effect
ion-pair association and solvent viscosity
questions.explanationEn: In the Debye–Hückel–Onsager equation, the solvent-drag counterflow of the ionic atmosphere produces the **electrophoretic retardation** ($A\sqrt{c}$, independent of $\Lambda_m^\circ$), while the finite time needed to rebuild the symmetric ionic atmosphere produces the **relaxation (asymmetry) effect** ($B\Lambda_m^\circ\sqrt{c}$).

questions.pyqTag: IIT JAM CY Topic • Physical Chemistry III: Chemical Kinetics, Electrochemistry & Adsorption (Set 01)
questions.questionTextEn: In simple hard-sphere collision theory for a bimolecular gas reaction, the rate constant is written as $k(T) = B T^{1/2} \exp(-E_0 / RT)$, where $B$ is independent of $T$ and $E_0$ is the threshold energy. The Arrhenius activation energy $E_a = RT^2 \frac{d\ln k}{dT}$ is related to $E_0$ by
optionsEn: $E_a = E_0 + RT$
questions.explanationEn: Taking the natural logarithm gives $\ln k = \ln B + \frac{1}{2}\ln T - \frac{E_0}{RT}$. Differentiating with respect to $T$: $\frac{d\ln k}{dT} = \frac{1}{2T} + \frac{E_0}{RT^2}$. Multiplying by $RT^2$ yields $E_a = E_0 + \frac{1}{2}RT$.

questions.pyqTag: IIT JAM CY Topic • Physical Chemistry III: Chemical Kinetics, Electrochemistry & Adsorption (Set 01)
questions.questionTextEn: Which of the following statement(s) about electrolyte conductivity in water at $298\text{ K}$ is/are correct?
optionsEn: For strong electrolytes at very low concentration, $\Lambda_m$ decreases linearly with $\sqrt{c}$.
For weak electrolytes, $\Lambda_m^\circ$ cannot be determined accurately by linear extrapolation of $\Lambda_m$ versus $\sqrt{c}$ to $c = 0$.
The limiting molar conductivity of $\text{BaCl}_2$ is $\lambda^\circ(\text{Ba}^{2+}) + 2\lambda^\circ(\text{Cl}^-)$.
Increasing temperature decreases the molar conductivity of aqueous $\text{KCl}$ due to increased ion collisions.
questions.explanationEn: (A), (B), and (C) are correct. Raising temperature lowers the viscosity of water and increases ionic mobility, so $\Lambda_m$ of aqueous $\text{KCl}$ **increases** with temperature, making (D) false.

questions.pyqTag: IIT JAM CY Topic • Physical Chemistry III: Chemical Kinetics, Electrochemistry & Adsorption (Set 01)
questions.questionTextEn: According to the Debye–Hückel limiting law ($\log_{10}\gamma_\pm = -A|z_+ z_-|\sqrt{I}$) for dilute aqueous solutions at $298\text{ K}$, the correct statement(s) is/are
optionsEn: At the same ionic strength $I$, $\gamma_\pm(\text{MgSO}_4) < \gamma_\pm(\text{CaCl}_2) < \gamma_\pm(\text{NaCl})$.
At the same low molality $m$, $\text{Na}_2\text{SO}_4$ and $\text{CaCl}_2$ have the same ionic strength $I = 3m$.
The limiting law predicts $\gamma_\pm < 1$ for all dilute electrolytes.
The limiting law remains quantitatively accurate at concentrations above $1.0\text{ M}$.
questions.explanationEn: $|z_+ z_-|$ is $4$ for $\text{MgSO}_4$, $2$ for $\text{CaCl}_2$, and $1$ for $\text{NaCl}$, so at fixed $I$, $\gamma_\pm$ decreases in the order $\text{NaCl} > \text{CaCl}_2 > \text{MgSO}_4$ (A true). Both 1:2 and 2:1 electrolytes have $I = \frac{1}{2}[m(4) + 2m(1)] = 3m$ (B true), and $-A|z_+z_-|\sqrt{I} < 0 \implies \gamma_\pm < 1$ (C true). The limiting law breaks down well below $0.01\text{ M}$ (D false).

questions.pyqTag: IIT JAM CY Topic • Physical Chemistry III: Chemical Kinetics, Electrochemistry & Adsorption (Set 01)
questions.questionTextEn: In the Lindemann–Hinshelwood mechanism for unimolecular reactions ($A + M \xrightleftharpoons[k_{-1}]{k_1} A^* + M$, $A^* \xrightarrow{k_2} P$), the correct statement(s) is/are
optionsEn: At very low pressures, collisional activation is rate-determining and the reaction is second order.
At very high pressures, unimolecular decomposition of $A^*$ is rate-determining and the reaction is first order.
Addition of an inert bath gas $M$ at low pressure increases the effective unimolecular rate constant $k_{\text{uni}}$.
The Lindemann mechanism predicts a strictly linear plot of $k_{\text{uni}}$ versus $[M]$ across all pressures.
questions.explanationEn: From $k_{\text{uni}} = \frac{k_1 k_2 [M]}{k_{-1}[M] + k_2}$, low $[M]$ gives second-order rate $k_1[A][M]$ (A true, C true) and high $[M]$ gives first-order rate $(k_1 k_2/k_{-1})[A]$ (B true). $k_{\text{uni}}$ vs $[M]$ is hyperbolic, not linear (only $1/k_{\text{uni}}$ vs $1/[M]$ is linear), so (D) is false.

questions.pyqTag: IIT JAM CY Topic • Physical Chemistry III: Chemical Kinetics, Electrochemistry & Adsorption (Set 01)
questions.questionTextEn: Consider the Gibbs adsorption equation $\Gamma_2 = -\frac{c}{RT}\left(\frac{\partial \gamma}{\partial c}\right)_T$ for dilute aqueous solutions. The correct statement(s) is/are
optionsEn: For an ionic surfactant of type $\text{R}^-\text{Na}^+$ in the absence of excess supporting electrolyte, the denominator becomes $2RT$.
If excess inert salt (e.g., $\text{NaCl}$) is added to an ionic surfactant solution, the denominator reverts to $RT$.
Strong inorganic electrolytes like $\text{NaCl}$ typically show $\Gamma_2 < 0$ at the air–water interface.
Above the critical micelle concentration (CMC), $\left(\frac{\partial \gamma}{\partial c}\right)_T$ becomes very large and negative.
questions.explanationEn: For a 1:1 ionic surfactant without excess salt, chemical potential involves $2RT\ln c$, giving $\Gamma_2 = -\frac{c}{2RT}(\partial\gamma/\partial c)_T$ (A true); excess salt screens the counterion term back to $RT$ (B true). Inorganic salts raise $\gamma$, giving $\Gamma_2 < 0$ (C true). Above the CMC, monomer activity stays nearly constant so $\gamma$ plateaus and $(\partial\gamma/\partial c)_T \approx 0$ (D false).

questions.pyqTag: IIT JAM CY Topic • Physical Chemistry III: Chemical Kinetics, Electrochemistry & Adsorption (Set 01)
questions.questionTextEn: Given $E^\circ(\text{Ag}^+/\text{Ag}) = +0.80\text{ V}$ and $E^\circ(\text{Ni}^{2+}/\text{Ni}) = -0.25\text{ V}$ at $298\text{ K}$, the standard EMF $E^\circ_{\text{cell}}$ of the spontaneous galvanic cell formed by these two half-cells is _______ $\text{V}$. *(round off to two decimal places)*
questions.explanationEn: $E^\circ_{\text{cell}} = E^\circ_{\text{cathode}} - E^\circ_{\text{anode}} = 0.80 - (-0.25) = 1.05\text{ V}$.

questions.pyqTag: IIT JAM CY Topic • Physical Chemistry III: Chemical Kinetics, Electrochemistry & Adsorption (Set 01)
questions.questionTextEn: For a dilute aqueous solution of a non-ionic surfactant at $300\text{ K}$, $\left(\frac{\partial \gamma}{\partial c}\right)_T = -0.30\text{ N m}^{-1}\text{ M}^{-1}$ at $c = 0.020\text{ M}$. Using $R = 8.314\text{ J K}^{-1}\text{ mol}^{-1}$, the Gibbs surface excess $\Gamma_2$ is _______ $\mu\text{mol m}^{-2}$. *(round off to two decimal places)*
questions.explanationEn: $\Gamma_2 = -\frac{c}{RT}\left(\frac{\partial \gamma}{\partial c}\right)_T = -\frac{0.020}{8.314 \times 300}(-0.30) = 2.406 \times 10^{-6}\text{ mol m}^{-2} = 2.41\ \mu\text{mol m}^{-2}$.

questions.pyqTag: IIT JAM CY Topic • Physical Chemistry III: Chemical Kinetics, Electrochemistry & Adsorption (Set 01)
questions.questionTextEn: A first-order radioactive decay has a half-life of $15\text{ min}$. The time required for $87.5\%$ of the sample to decay is _______ $\text{min}$. *(answer in integer)*
questions.explanationEn: When $87.5\%$ has decayed, $12.5\% = \frac{1}{8} = \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^3$ remains, corresponding to $3$ half-lives: $t = 3 \times 15 = 45\text{ min}$.

questions.pyqTag: IIT JAM CY Topic • Physical Chemistry III: Chemical Kinetics, Electrochemistry & Adsorption (Set 01)
questions.questionTextEn: At $298\text{ K}$, the limiting molar conductivities of $\text{HCl}$, $\text{CH}_3\text{COONa}$, and $\text{NaCl}$ are $426.1$, $91.0$, and $126.5\text{ S cm}^2\text{ mol}^{-1}$, respectively. The limiting molar conductivity of $\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}$ at $298\text{ K}$ is _______ $\text{S cm}^2\text{ mol}^{-1}$. *(round off to one decimal place)*
questions.explanationEn: $\Lambda_m^\circ(\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}) = \Lambda_m^\circ(\text{HCl}) + \Lambda_m^\circ(\text{CH}_3\text{COONa}) - \Lambda_m^\circ(\text{NaCl}) = 426.1 + 91.0 - 126.5 = 390.6\text{ S cm}^2\text{ mol}^{-1}$.

questions.pyqTag: IIT JAM CY Topic • Physical Chemistry III: Chemical Kinetics, Electrochemistry & Adsorption (Set 01)
questions.questionTextEn: A species $A$ decays by two parallel first-order routes with rate constants $k_1 = 0.0200\text{ s}^{-1}$ and $k_2 = 0.0493\text{ s}^{-1}$. The overall half-life of $A$ is _______ $\text{s}$. *(round off to one decimal place)*
questions.explanationEn: The effective decay constant is $k_{\text{eff}} = k_1 + k_2 = 0.0693\text{ s}^{-1}$, so $t_{1/2} = \frac{\ln 2}{0.0693} = 10.00\text{ s} \approx 10.0\text{ s}$.

questions.pyqTag: IIT JAM CY Topic • Physical Chemistry III: Chemical Kinetics, Electrochemistry & Adsorption (Set 01)
questions.questionTextEn: For the second-order reaction $A + B \to P$ ($r = k[A][B]$) with $k = 0.50\text{ dm}^3\text{ mol}^{-1}\text{ min}^{-1}$, $[A]_0 = 0.20\text{ M}$, and $[B]_0 = 0.10\text{ M}$, the concentration of $B$ remaining after $20\text{ min}$ is _______ $\text{M}$. *(round off to three decimal places)*
